title: Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school
description: As the new school year begins in Austria, a law banning headscarves in schools for girls under 14 has gone into force.The law forbids "traditional Mus
body: As the new school year begins in Austria, a law banning headscarves in schools for girls under 14 has gone into force.The law forbids "traditional Muslim" head coverings, such as hijabs or burkas, in public and private schools across the country.Integration Minister Claudia Bauer, from the conservative People's Party (ÖVP), says the headscarf is "a sign of oppression and a means of controlling girls from the earliest childhood".But critics say the new law is fuelling anti-Muslim feeling in the country and could be unconstitutional.The law was brought in by the conservative-led coalition of three centrist parties, the ÖVP, the Social Democrats (SPÖ) and the liberal Neos. They say the law is a "clear commitment to gender equality" and is intended to protect the rights of young girls.Carla Amina Baghajati, from the official Islamic Community in Austria (IGGÖ), told the BBC that the organisation "firmly opposes the ban"."We believe it unjustifiably restricts the fundamental right to freedom of religion and disproportionately affects Muslim girls," she said."Rather than protecting children, it singles out a specific religious practice and risks excluding the very children it claims to support."The IGGÖ said it would support legal challenges by girls and their families "who believe that their fundamental rights are being infringed" and who wished to bring their cases before the Constitutional Court. The court struck down a previous ban on headscarves in primary schools in 2020 on the basis that it contravened the principle of Austria's religious neutrality.Teachers are expected to enforce the new ban if they see a child wearing a headscarf by holding a series of talks with the student and their legal guardians.If there are repeated violations, child services must be notified and as a last resort, guardians could face fines of up to €800 (£685).Some teachers have expressed concerns about having to enforce the ban.The Green Party's Sigi Maurer accused Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr, from the liberal NEOS, of "creating new conflicts and offloading them onto the teachers".She said teachers were "already under enormous strain" and that Wiederkehr wanted to "foist the role of police officers onto them" on top of their other duties.The opposition far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) says the current ban doesn't go far enough. It is calling for a general prohibition on headscarves and face coverings in schools for students and teachers alike.The FPÖ's Ricarda Berger said there was "no place for political Islam in Austria, and certainly not in our schools".Austria's Chancellor Christian Stocker, leader of the ÖVP, recently called for a constitutional ban on political Islam, telling Austrian public broadcaster ORF he did not "want to live in an Islamic state".In France there has been a ban on wearing any conspicuous religious symbols, including headscarves, turbans and kippas, in schools for more than 20 years.The Austrian law differs from French legislation in that it specifically targets head coverings worn by Muslim women.Austria, like several other European countries including France, Belgium and Denmark, bans the full face veil (niqabs or burkas) in public.Baghajati said the IGGÖ was concerned about "a troubling trend" across Europe "in which complex social challenges are reduced to symbolic measures aimed at minority groups.""Such approaches may generate political attention, but they rarely solve the underlying problems," she said.

schema.headline: Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school

title: China to pump $54bn into state banks and insurers to boost economy
description: China is pumping tens of billions of dollars into eight state-owned banks and insurance companies to help shore up the country's financial system and
body: China is pumping tens of billions of dollars into eight state-owned banks and insurance companies to help shore up the country's financial system and boost its slowing economy.The cash injection, which is being led by China's finance ministry, will total 360 billion yuan ($53.6bn; £39.7bn), state news agency Xinhua said on Sunday.The outlet said the move "will help further enhance their sound operating capabilities, risk resistance capabilities, and ability to serve the real economy".It marks the latest move in Beijing's attempts to reinvigorate the world's second largest economy as it faces issues including trade tensions with the West, the impact of the Iran war and an aging population.The package will boost the finances of three big lenders and five insurers including the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, the Agricultural Bank of China and China Export & Credit Insurance Corporation.State news outlet Global Times said this "will give banks and financial institutions more resources to channel into credit for the real economy, while strengthening their ability to withstand external shocks at a time of global financial uncertainty".President Xi Jinping has long seen financial stability as key to China's national security.This weekend's announcements come as Beijing is aiming to reshape the economy in the face of a number of challenges such as a shrinking workforce, a years-long property market slump and ongoing trade and technology rivalry with the US.China's economic growth slowed sharply between the start of April and end of June as weak domestic demand and the Iran war's impact on oil prices overshadowed the country's strong exports.Official gross domestic product (GDP) figures released in July showed China's economy grew in the second quarter by 4.3%, below Beijing's annual target, and after a 5% rise in the first quarter.In March, Beijing cut the growth target to a range of 4.5%-5%, its lowest economic expansion goal since 1991, a move some analysts say has given Beijing space to acknowledge pre-existing economic weakness.

schema.headline: China to pump $54bn into state banks and insurers to boost economy

title: Nepal holds national day of mourning for victims of flash flood disaster
description: Nepalis observed a national day of mourning for the victims of the flash flood on Monday, lighting candles to mark the last day of the traditional 13-
body: Nepalis observed a national day of mourning for the victims of the flash flood on Monday, lighting candles to mark the last day of the traditional 13-day Hindu mourning period. While flags were flown at half mast, commemorations were scaled back as rescue teams continue to search for survivors. Candlelight vigils were planned for Monday evening. At least 1,287 people are known to have died after a flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through villages in a Himalayan valley along the border between Nepal and Tibet. Almost two weeks later, more than 5,000 people are still missing. Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) told the Reuters news agency that there would be "no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas."Nepal's president, Ram Chandra Paudel, toured areas devastated by the floods on Monday, an aide told Reuters. The home ministry said that government offices, as well as missions abroad, would fly the national flag at half mast to mark the final day of the mourning period. Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepali teams, said in an update on X that the operation meant facing "multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties and lives that may still be saved."Four people have been rescued in recent days, three at hydropower stations or tunnels. On Saturday, a 64-year-old Nepali woman was pulled from her buried house on Saturday, more than 10 days after a wall of ice, rock and mud partially buried her house in the Nuwakot district. She was discovered alive on the fourth floor of the building by Nepal's Armed Police Force and airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment. On Sunday rescue workers in China recovered twelve bodies in the Nepal-Tibet border, using excavators, shovels and ground penetrating radar at the site.  At least 5,083 people are still missing in Nepal. On the Tibetan side, the death toll reported by Chinese media on Friday was 31, with 531 people unaccounted for.

schema.headline: Nepal holds national day of mourning for victims of flash flood disaster

title: Indonesia volcano eruption leaves 340,000 stranded as airports extend closure
description: Halim Perdanakusuma, a smaller airport that caters to civil and military flights, will also remain closed until then.Snaking queues formed at the depa
body: Halim Perdanakusuma, a smaller airport that caters to civil and military flights, will also remain closed until then.Snaking queues formed at the departure halls in Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly.Finna, who was supposed to fly home to Jakarta from Malang, a city in East Java, on Sunday morning, described the frezny at the airport as flights got repeatedly rescheduled."It was very crowded because passengers from the morning flights had piled up, while those scheduled for later departures still didn't know what would happen," the 46-year-old told BBC Indonesian. "We were all glued to the flight information screens."Not wanting to deal with the uncertainty, Finna eventually spent the night on two intercity trains before arriving in Jakarta at 03:00 on Monday."Everyone seems to be racking their brains [figuring alternative transportation options]", said Jo Shaw, who was visiting Indonesia with members of her conservation charity Save the Rhino International. Shaw's team had axed their plans to camp out at Java's Ujung Kulon National Park after authorities raised its alert level for the Anak Krakatau volcano."Being stranded in an airport hotel is a relatively minor inconvenience to be resolved in a few days hopefully," Shaw said, adding that she was more concerned about the teams working on the ground with the rhinos under such environmental conditions.A newly wed Malaysian couple who had just spent a week in Bali said they were told that the next flight back to Kuala Lumpur wouldn't be until 11 September."What are we going to do here for another five days? We only prepared enough money for our honeymoon and [were supposed] to go home yesterday," Amir Hamzah told Malaysia's national news agency Bernama."We thought we would just sleep at the airport for a few hours and then take the morning flight home [on Monday]. We never thought we would end up being stuck here for days," the 29-year-old said.On Monday, Indonesia's Geological Agency warned that "the probability of further eruptions in the coming periods remains high".Volcanic ash reached as high as 6,000m on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000m on the Sumatra side and in some parts of Java's westernmost province Banten, the meteorological agency BMKG said.Anak Krakatau sits on the Sunda Strait about midway between the islands of Java and Sumatra.The most recent eruption occurred at 20:23 on Sunday, according to the agency."We ‌cannot ascertain when this ‌will end due to the dynamic weather," Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said in relation to the temporary closures of the affected airports.Dudy said on Sunday that authorities across the airports have been conducting tests every 30 minutes "to anticipate whether the ash spread is widening or subsiding".Authorities have warned against approaching or engaging in activities within a 3km radius from the active crater, while ships passing through the Sunda Strait have also been prohibited from entering an exclusion zone of 3km radius from it.Authorities have also confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano.Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.The volcano collapsed in December 2018 triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java.Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high.The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand.Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that's 452 individual active volcanoes.With reporting by Farida Susanty in Jakarta and Koh Ewe in Singapore

title: Peace talks rich in symbolism but differences between Russia and Ukraine remain
description: Image source, ReutersByDiplomatic correspondentThe talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian
body: Image source, ReutersByDiplomatic correspondentThe talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion. The fact they had to travel by train because they could not risk flying and running the gauntlet of Russian drones - weapons launched on the orders of the man at whose table they sat in the Kremlin only hours ago. The symbolism of Ukrainian President Zelensky greeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's Saint Sophia Cathedral, not only an icon of Ukraine's ancient history, but also just a few yards from where Russian drones hit the headquarters of the country's security services on Friday. You did not have to join too many dots to work out the point Zelensky was making.Both sides held talks for several hours; they were later joined by some European national security advisers, including the UK's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell. And afterwards, all sides spoke warmly of having held substantive discussions. They spoke hopefully of reviving past "trilateral talks" involving both the US and Europe.Image source, ReutersBut fundamental differences remain. The US envoys had come hot foot from Moscow where Vladimir Putin had told them Russia was making "tangible advances" on the battlefield. The story they heard from Ukraine was different, in fact the opposite. Ukrainian officials claim that in August they gained more territory than they lost and Russia suffered 42,000 casualties, dead or wounded.Putin had also told the US envoys the root causes of the conflict had to be addressed, shorthand for his longstanding strategic demands that Ukraine cede territory, abandon hopes of joining Nato and reduce the size of its army.After the talks, Zelensky insisted Ukraine would require "strong and clear" security guarantees, including a strong army. Nor did he give any sign of being willing to give up any territory in the eastern Donbas region, an issue he described dryly as "difficult".Figure caption, Watch: President Zelensky welcomes US envoys in KyivWitkoff insisted progress had been made and the ingredients for a settlement were there. But he admitted both sides would have to make compromises to narrow the differences between them. And right now, it is hard to see either side doing that.So for now, the expectation in Kyiv is that the fighting will continue and they will face a hard winter ahead. Some diplomats talk of a window of opportunity for a possible settlement next spring. Others are less optimistic. Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit because the short-term pause in air strikes agreed by both sides had given the people of Kyiv a brief respite. Few expect it to last for long.Figure caption, Watch: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner say they are "encouraged" by Ukraine talks

title: Europe wrestles with impact of historic regional gains for Germany’s AfD
description: "Seismic", "a socio-political earthquake", "a watershed moment for Germany".This was how political analysts and many media outlets described the stunn
body: "Seismic", "a socio-political earthquake", "a watershed moment for Germany".This was how political analysts and many media outlets described the stunning victory of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in local elections in Germany on Sunday. Is that an exaggeration?Saxony-Anhalt is one of the smallest of massive Germany's 16 regions. It boasts a mere 1.7 million out of 59 million eligible voters nationwide. How significant can its political sentiments be, especially since the AfD narrowly failed to win an outright majority?The answer: Very significant.First and foremost, at home in Germany.The vote may have been regional but it impacts at national level. The AfD landslide piles even more pressure on the already beleaguered centrist coalition government in Berlin. It may prove to be the nail in the political coffin of Germany's deeply unpopular conservative Chancellor, Friedrich Merz. He had promised to slash the AfD's popularity.These political woes will further weaken and distract Germany, the EU's most powerful player, at a time of continental crisis - as Europe struggles to contain Russian aggression, US President Donald Trump's tariff tantrums and the economic threat from China.The Saxony-Anhalt result also provokes soul-searching throughout Germany, where the Nazi past still looms large. This is the first outstanding electoral landslide for a hard-right nationalist party - giving it a real shot at governing, in this case, at regional level - since the fall of the Third Reich in 1945.The German authorities have labelled the AfD, in part, anti-democratic and a number of regional factions of the party, including Saxony-Anhalt, far-right extremist.The AfD is well-known to be particularly popular in east Germany but it is now also polling as the biggest political party nationwide.Germany's political mainstream has failed voters, it would seem. What does Europe's biggest single economy, its most populous nation not counting Russia, do now?Tiny Saxony-Anhalt is causing waves outside Germany, too.None other than the US president swiftly posted the Saxony-Anhalt exit poll on his Truth Social platform on Sunday.The AfD's anti-immigration, anti-woke, "Germany for Germans" message chimes closely with Donald Trump's Maga [Make America Great Again] missive. Along with a number of other nationalist parties in Europe, the AfD borrows heavily from the Trump playbook - undermining mainstream media, questioning the neutrality of judges and promising to "make Germany great again".Interesting to note though - the US president is rarely name-checked on the campaign trail in Europe. Politicians are keenly aware just how unpopular he is amongst voters.Hot on Donald Trump's social media heels on Sunday night was the influential Russian businessman Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund. He declared the AfD result "historic", Germany's national government "discredited" and the German chancellor "humiliated", comparing Friedrich Merz to the UK's not-long-gone Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, who felt forced to resign this summer.Also watching the Saxony-Anhalt election closely was the European Union. The next 12 months is bumper election season across the EU. Ballots are expected in key nations France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Brussels fears more "extreme" parties, left but particularly right of the political spectrum, may benefit across the board.The leader of Spain's nationalist Vox party, Santiago Abascal, posted on X on Sunday that the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt was " a great hope for Germany and for Europe".By contrast, France's Europe Minister, Benjamin Haddad, an ally of centrist President Emmanuel Macron, warned "this is a serious moment in Europe, seeing the far-right win in a regional election in Germany".Neither the AfD, nor other European parties labelled "extreme right" or "hard right", accept the label. They also differ from one another in tone and party programme. France's National Rally under Marine Le Pen kicked the AfD out of its grouping in the European Parliament two years ago, for being too "radical". What the parties do tend to share, however, is an anti-immigration platform and strong nationalist messaging. And that really worries the EU.Whether it is a rallying cry for "Germany First" or "Italy First" or "France for the French!", the concern in Brussels is that the rise of nationalist parties strains European cohesion at a time when outside events demand it more than ever.Nationalist parties like the AfD or Italy's League Party tend to be deeply Eurosceptic, but Brussels says Europe needs to stand united to counter Donald Trump's bullying, for example, or to effectively protect European business against China's goods dumping.Europe's defence establishment also warns that fractures in European sanctions against Russia or countries going tepid on Nato membership (as you see in Marine Le Pen's National Rally for example, or Germany's AfD) just emboldens Moscow.Security chiefs say nations must stick together to stop Russia in Ukraine, otherwise the Kremlin will be tempted to attack inside Nato, such as the Baltic states.The thing is, Europe's voters are very aware of these outside threats and the impact they have at home. They worry about the impact of wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, about crumbling health services at home and dwindling economic security for themselves and their families. Uncontrolled immigration and safety on the streets are huge concerns, too.And this is where the significance of the Saxony-Anhalt vote shines bright - a flashing red warning to traditional political parties, but also to institutions across Europe like the judiciary and security services. Those the AfD dismisses as the self-interested "Establishment".Voters on this continent feel lost and let down by parties they have supported over and again for decades. Looking right or left now at election time does not mean they have all suddenly become extremist.The AfD campaign slogan in Saxony-Anhalt was an upbeat "Anything is Possible!" - plus a promise to make Germans feel proud of their country again. Till now untried and untested in government, people seem increasingly willing to give them a go.

schema.headline: Europe wrestles with impact of historic regional gains for Germany’s AfD

title: Indonesia fires: The volunteer firefighters risking their lives to defuse 'carbon bombs'
description: The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs'Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fahrin Ramadhianto has
body: The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs'Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fahrin Ramadhianto has been fighting Borneo's wildfires for a month - and noticing the impacts on his body.ByGavin Butler and Ahmad DhaniReporting fromBanjarbaru, KalimantanThe sky grows heavy in Borneo, though not with rain. The air, amber-hued and treacle-thick, is smudged under a blanket of smog that has spilled across international borders – to Singapore, Manila, Kuala Lumpur. Down on the ground, smoke steams from the soil.It's like tear gas, says Dwi Sujatmoko."It hits your nose straight away, your eyes burn – that's more or less what it's like," he says. "People say these fires are extraordinary because of the flames and the smoke. And they're right."The 35-year-old volunteer firefighter has spent more than a month enveloped in this haze, breathing toxic millennia-old microparticles of carbon as he toils against a seemingly inextinguishable fire front.Using hand tools, carts and portable fire pumps, he and thousands of other volunteer firefighters – many of them indigenous Dayak or Banjar people – are up against an inferno that has carbonised some 200,000 hectares of forest and farmland across Indonesian Borneo since early July. Underground and out of sight, giant subterranean peat fires continue to smoulder, choking the air with poisonous fumes."Once a fire becomes uncontrolled, it harms many people. Not just humans, but also animals and plants," Sujatmoko says. "If underground fire spreads and can no longer be controlled, the losses are enormous."Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fires have torched some 200,000 hectares across Indonesian Borneo since early JulyIndonesia is in the throes of a wildfire catastrophe.Amid a so-called "Super El Niño" that has supercharged local drought conditions, thousands of active fire hotspots are spreading and multiplying across the country, fuelling a transnational haze crisis that is the region's worst in more than a decade.But what makes Borneo's fires particularly worrying is the fact that they are burning through one of the world's largest tropical peatland ecosystems.This 4.5-million-hectare swathe of forest and swamp, under normal conditions, serves as a valuable reservoir for ancient carbon.When these peatlands catch fire, they risk releasing millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane into the atmosphere – a "pulse" of greenhouse gas emissions that has earned them the sobriquet of "carbon bomb"."Peatlands are incredibly effective carbon stores because their waterlogged conditions slow decomposition, allowing carbon to accumulate underground for thousands of years," explains Dr Nisa Novita, a peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN)."But this also means they can become a 'carbon bomb' when they are drained or burned, because that carbon can be rapidly released into the atmosphere."Tropical peatlands in Indonesia are among the world's most effective natural carbon stores. The deeper the peat, the greater the carbon stock – and in Kalimantan, we have found peat deposits that can exceed 20 metres in depth."A peatland that deep has been known to harbour more than 6,000 tonnes of carbon – roughly equivalent to the annual CO₂ emissions of 4,800 cars – per hectare. And when it burns, says Dr Nisa, that fossilised carbon can be released into the atmosphere "very rapidly".Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, "We're doing everything we can to help deal with this haze disaster because it's our duty," says firefighter Dwi SujatmokoThe toxic cloudThousands of people across South East Asia are now feeling the effects of those emissions in their eyes, chests and throats. Across Indonesia as well as Brunei, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines, air pollution indices have soared to "unhealthy" extremes - almost 75 times the World Health Organization's recommended level, in some cases – and hospital admissions have surged.Between July and August, Indonesia's Health Ministry recorded over 50,000 cases of respiratory infections linked to land and forest fires. More than 12,000 of them were children under the age of five."Everybody who's living within that pollution cloud is breathing in the products of those smouldering peat fires," says Susan Page, a professor at the University of Leicester's school of geology and the environment, who's been researching peatlands in Asia for three decades."They're breathing in carbon monoxide, which is toxic, and they're breathing in the very finely divided particulate matter... [which] can pass through the alveoli in the lungs into the bloodstream and cause further problems elsewhere in the body, including issues with the heart."Living in this kind of pollution cloud is extremely unhealthy."Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fighting peat fires requires saturating the ground so thoroughly that it becomes "like porridge"Nowhere are these health impacts being felt more acutely than at the coalface of the disaster: the fire front.Here, volunteer firefighters have been risking their lives and lungs to extinguish burning peatlands which are notoriously difficult to put out. Two volunteers  in Central Kalimantan have died in recent days, reportedly after their health deteriorated from putting out fires.Cloaked in toxic haze that can burn years off a person's lifespan, volunteers have been digging ponds, canals and borewells through bone-dry peat in a desperate attempt to keep their hoses tapped. Some have been driving pipes into the earth, making ad hoc irrigation systems to combat subterranean fires. Others have been sleeping within a stone's throw of the frontline so they can battle the blazes through the night."The worst thing here has been the smoke," says Fahrin Ramadhianto, a volunteer firefighter in South Kalimantan's Banjarbaru, one of the worst-hit areas. "The smell is like decaying wood being burned – that's the characteristic smell of peat. And that peat contains decomposed wood and organic material from many different sources."An unnatural imbalanceIndonesia's peatland fires are not a new phenomenon. Experts say the crisis is rooted in decades of land-use change, dating back to the Suharto era, when vast areas of rainforest and peatland in Kalimantan were opened for logging, plantations and large-scale development projects.Yet authorities have historically avoided blaming industrial actors for causing large-scale fires. Instead, the same indigenous communities who are now engaged in firefighting operations across the island have often been accused of triggering the blazes, due to traditional farming methods that use controlled burns to clear away vegetation.Tono, a representative of the Dayak Kanayatn people of West Kalimantan, told the BBC that Dayak communities are frequently used as scapegoats, despite carrying out land clearing with extensive planning, caution and adherence to multi-generational customs. Tono says these communities' traditional practices, known as uma bukit or "hill farming", are rooted in the idea of maintaining balance with nature.Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, "The worst thing here has been the smoke," says Fahrin RamadhiantoBut the natural balance is fast unravelling in Kalimantan, the most deforested area in Indonesia. The region lost almost 160,000 hectares of forest area in 2025, more than one-third of the nationwide figure – much of it to make way for plantations and monocrop agriculture.It is these same industrial-scale development projects that have been largely responsible for draining the area's peat swamps, which renders them significantly more fire-prone, Prof Page says."Peatlands aren't really the ideal place to set up a plantation – but of course, once the more suitable mineral soils had been exhausted it became possible, by using large machinery, to drain the peatlands and create conditions which would be dry enough," she says."So not only have you got the deforestation, but peatland drainage of course has also greatly increased the fire risk."Page also points out that, whether on fire or not, a drained peatland emits carbon dioxide into the atmosphere "all of the time"."I think that's forgotten," she says. "I think it's important to recognise that when we see the fires, they're like a dramatic example of what is actually going on the whole time in a drained peatland... The fires are just the worst expression of [that]."Now, as these latest fires continue to spiral out of control, Sujatmoko and others face a concatenation of difficulties in the coming days, weeks and months – not least of which is a shortage of water. Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Drainage and drought in Indonesia's peatlands has exacerbated their vulnerability to fire Fighting peat fires requires saturating the ground so thoroughly that it becomes "like porridge", Sujatmoko explains.Even then there is a high chance the fire will reappear, like a smoking revenant, fed by hidden fuel buried in the invisible depths of the peat swamp.In the face of these persistent reignitions, ongoing drought conditions and toxic smog, fatigue is another concern."We're definitely tired," says Sujatmoko. "We get exhausted, we miss our families, our children, our wives. But for now, all of us are putting those things aside. We're doing everything we can to help deal with this haze disaster because it's our duty.""We also hope rain comes soon," he adds. "We've spent months away from home... May all the efforts of those on the front lines be a blessing for everyone."Additional reporting by Faisal Irfani from BBC Indonesian.

schema.headline: Indonesia fires: The volunteer firefighters risking their lives to defuse 'carbon bombs'

title: Germany's AfD calls for parties to work with it after Saxony-Anhalt win
description: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, its deputy parliamentary lead
body: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, its deputy parliamentary leader has told the BBC, after a historic victory in elections there.  Sunday's preliminary results show it fell three seats short of an outright majority, with 43.8% of the vote. It is now seeking support from other parties or individuals in order to govern.While most German political parties refuse to work with the AfD, Beatrix von Storch called for its opponents to enter talks and said: "You cannot say, I do not accept the vote of the people". Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was "deeply shocked" by the result, describing it as "seismic... not just in the country but also in my own political party and I take that very seriously".His party, the conservative CDU, saw its share of the vote almost halved to 17.2% in the state's preliminary results.Merz said it was not possible to return to "business as usual", adding that the country needed "profound reforms" and the CDU needed to "reach people at an emotional level". No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing and local education.Von Storch said the state's results "were on the table and now democrats have to talk to [one] another. This is what democracy demands".She added that if parties refused to work with the AfD, "then we might end up in severe chaos and maybe we have a new election".Her comments were echoed by AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, who told a news conference on Monday that the party had won a "clear mandate to govern".The state's defeated premier, the CDU's Sven Schulze, also said the mandate to govern Saxony-Anhalt "now lies with the AfD".Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.The party's plans for Saxony-Anhalt, which include segregating child refugees into special classes and setting up a task-force to help detain and deport migrants who no longer have the right to be in the state, are highly controversial within Germany.The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority, although the result has not yet been finalised.Von Storch told the BBC the AfD was talking to individuals within the CDU group - the largest party in both the state's outgoing coalition and Germany's government - because they were "very, very unhappy with their own party".One idea being floated is an informal deal whereby a small party - the BSW - could give their tacit support to allow the AfD to form a minority government.The left-wing populist BSW, which is set to win five seats, is also tough on immigration and backs importing Russian gas.Siegmund said discussions with other parties were initiated on Sunday night and could potentially take days or weeks to conclude. "We reach out to everybody first, we will have consultations and then we'll see whether [there are] individual parliamentary groups or MPs who would be willing to help us," he added.Another possibility - at least in theory - is a messy, minority coalition government led by the conservative CDU party. But that appears very unlikely.There's also the prospect of another election to break the deadlock - an idea which has been mooted by Siegmund who has said he doesn't want to compromise on his policy goals.The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states. They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.Merz described the Saxony-Anhalt defeat as the worst the CDU had suffered "in years, if not decades", acknowledging that the results in upcoming regional elections in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and Berlin could have "increasing significance".Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. Commentators and political opponents called AfD's victory a watershed and break with the past. "This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters overnight. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."On Sunday, US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the state's projected results on his Truth Social platform. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev then took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD".Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.Polish centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk saw the result very differently, saying "in Poland only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD".Asked about those who had expressed fears over the far-right party gaining power in the state, deputy parliamentary leader Beatrix von Storch told the BBC that its supporters were afraid of "losing our economy, they are afraid of losing our inner security".She said conservative voters were turning to alternative political parties because they were not being listened to.She added that the party's detractors should: "Wake up and realise what happened in several other European states... The conservative parties will disappear from the landscape as it happened in Italy, as it's about to happen in the UK, as it might also happen in France".

schema.headline: Germany's AfD calls for parties to work with it after Saxony-Anhalt win

title: Israeli strikes in southern Lebanese village kill 12
description: Israeli air strikes on a village in southern Lebanon have killed at least 12 people, the Lebanese health ministry says.Eleven people, including two ch
body: Israeli air strikes on a village in southern Lebanon have killed at least 12 people, the Lebanese health ministry says.Eleven people, including two children and four women, were killed in a strike that destroyed a residential building in Kfar Roummane overnight. A second strike on a vehicle killed a paramedic.The Israeli military said it struck infrastructure sites belonging to the Shia Muslim armed group Hezbollah, as well as "several terrorists" transferring weapons, in retaliation for a drone attack on troops in an occupied area of the country.Israeli attacks across southern Lebanon have killed at least 27 people over the past three days, according to the health ministry.Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said the "dangerous escalation" was jeopardising June's US-brokered ceasefire, which was meant to end the conflict between Israel and Hezbollah.He urged the international community to put pressure on Israel to stop the attacks.The Israeli military has intensified its strikes in southern Lebanon in recent days.They have happened in places near the strip of territory that is occupied by Israeli troops, and large numbers of residents have again been fleeing those areas.The latest attacks targeted Kfar Roummane, in Nabatieh district, which is only a few hundred metres from what the Israeli military calls its "security zone".The first air strike destroyed a three-storey residential building near the town's Shuyuiya roundabout shortly after midnight, Lebanon's state-run National News Agency reported.The Lebanese health ministry said that in addition to the 11 people killed, eight were injured, including three children and a paramedic from the Islamic Health Association, which is an emergency service linked to Hezbollah.The second strike hit a vehicle carrying paramedics from the Islamic Risala Scout Association, killing one of them and injuring two others, according to the ministry. The Risala Scouts is an emergency service affiliated with the Amal movement, a Shia group allied to Hezbollah.The health ministry said the death toll "serves as further irrefutable evidence of the grave violations of international humanitarian law committed by the Israeli occupation, targeting medics and children".A resident of Kfar Roummane, Sara Moallaem, 35, told the BBC that she had been asleep with her five children in their rental home when she heard the explosions.She immediately grabbed her children and moved them into the home's "safe room" while they waited for the booms and the sirens to stop.Some of those killed in the strikes were distant relatives of Sara's husband. She insisted they were civilians with no affiliation to Hezbollah.Sara said she was planning to move her family to the coastal city of Sidon for their safety."During the day, it is almost normal, [with] people going back and forth. But as it comes near the night, things escalate, and now my children are afraid and I am packing now for the sixth or seventh time. It is terrible," she explained."Now that they are targeting civilians, I don't want to weep for my children."The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it struck "several Hezbollah terrorist infrastructure sites across southern Lebanon" overnight after the group's fighters launched two explosive drones towards Israeli troops operating in the Ali al-Taher ridge area, which is just south of Kfar Roummane and inside the Israeli-declared "security zone"."Additionally, the IDF struck several terrorists who were identified transferring weapons in the area of Kfar Roummane, in order to remove the threat they posed to IDF soldiers.""The claim that several uninvolved individuals were harmed as a result of the strikes is being reviewed," it added.The IDF also said it had struck the Nabatieh area and killed several Hezbollah fighters on Sunday following a separate drone attack.Lebanon's health ministry said 11 people were killed in Israeli strikes across the south of the country on Sunday. They included nine people in Nabatieh al-Fawqa, which is south of Kfar Roummane, and two women in Arab Salim, to the north of the village.There was no immediate comment from Hezbollah. But on Sunday, one of the group's members of parliament, Ali Ammar, declared that "the language of resistance is the only language that is effective against the Israeli enemy".The ceasefire agreement between Lebanon, Israel and the US calls for Hezbollah to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon, and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area.Hezbollah has rejected the framework, saying the provisions linking Israel's withdrawal to the group's disarmament cross "all red lines".Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah - which is supported by Iran - launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader.Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south.At least 4,362 people have been killed in Lebanon during the conflict, including 395 women and 259 children, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians.Israeli authorities say 40 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed during the conflict.Additional reporting by Ghaith Solh

schema.headline: Israeli strikes in southern Lebanese village kill 12

title: Manchester United v Sabah: Meet Azerbaijani club's coach Valdas Dambrauskas
description: On Thursday, Valdas Dambrauskas will walk out at Old Trafford as manager of Sabah in the Champions League.The Lithuanian's career will come full circl
body: On Thursday, Valdas Dambrauskas will walk out at Old Trafford as manager of Sabah in the Champions League.The Lithuanian's career will come full circle, some 20 years since he made his first steps into coaching with Manchester United Soccer Schools."This is beyond my imagination," Dambrauskas told BBC Sport. "To go through that tunnel on to that pitch."I've been many times to Old Trafford with the kids, and now I'm going to come as a coach."This only scratches the surface of Dambrauskas' remarkable story.It begins with an appearance on the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, Dambrauskas using his modest winnings to move to London and forge a career in football.It is a tale of casual jobs, a determination to succeed and a nomadic coaching career across Europe - which now brings the 49-year-old back to England in the Champions League with the Azerbaijani club.As Sabah's players and staff celebrated reaching the Champions League two weeks ago, unbeknownst to Dambrauskas he was becoming a social media star.It all related to that appearance on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? in 2002.Not because he was on the show, but how he spent the money he won."This is so long ago," said Dambrauskas with a wry smile. "A back-in-the-year story that really was forgotten."And now suddenly everybody is speaking about this."Dambrauskas walked away with 4,000 litas (about £725). That might not sound like much, but it was six months' wages to the average Lithuanian.For Dambrauskas, the real story should be his career and not a game show."Everybody now takes only this part, you know, about the money," Dambrauskas said. "But yes, it is a true story. "My idea was somehow I will try to go on these [coaching] courses to gain the coaching badge, maybe go back one day to Lithuania and start to work as a football coach."What began with Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? would map out his whole career.'I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs'Dambrauskas says he had known since the age of 12 he would not make it as a player, but coaching would keep him close to football.He arrived in London in August 2002 aged 25 on a student visa with limited English.What followed would be eight years of hard work where he would coach for community projects, at a semi-professional club, within professional youth programmes - and hold down multiple jobs while raising two children. In 2004 he enrolled on a course in sports science and coaching at London Metropolitan University, the first real step in his career.Then he started out coaching by volunteering with the Access to Sports Project for deprived children in Finsbury Park.He went on to work with London Tigers, a charitable community organisation which runs teams from junior level right through to semi-professional.Starting out as a volunteer, across five years he progressed to manage the first team in non-league football in the Spartan South Midlands League, FA Cup and FA Vase.Dambrauskas became the first Lithuanian to achieve a Uefa coaching licence through the London Football Association."I went on every possible course, every possible conference, London Football Coaches Association meetings," Dambrauskas said. "Everywhere I could go just to gain some information, some knowledge, some extra diploma, extra course. "That was very important for me and I took my chances."He got his first break at a professional club when Manchester United Soccer Schools took a chance on him in 2004.Dambrauskas spent five years coaching on residential courses in the UK and in Europe."That was the best thing that could happen in my life," Dambrauskas said."I went through three or four interviews. I will be forever grateful to [Foundation chief executive] John Shiels, the way he gave me this chance, because I didn't have experience."I'd never been in a place with so many great personalities as I got in the Manchester United Soccer Schools."After a short spell with Fulham, Dambrauskas moved to Brentford. He credits academy director Ose Aibangee as one of the biggest influences on his career, pushing his limits.All the while he was juggling home life and working multiple jobs to make ends meet. "I was a gardener, a handyman, doing newspaper rounds at the beginning, also polishing floors in a pub," Dambrauskas said."So many jobs. Working in retail, and then as a sports development officer, then a sports development manager, and the central YMCA."I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs."As well as the trip to Manchester United this week, Sabah will complete their Champions League group games at Arsenal in January. This also feels like fate for Dambrauskas - one of the buildings at London Metropolitan University on Holloway Road overlooked Emirates Stadium. When asked about his time in England, Dambrauskas' face lights up. "When I hear this word 'England', it for me sounds like opportunities," Dambrauskas said."It was really amazing. England gave me all this and I'll forever be grateful."Dambrauskas was working three jobs - at Brentford, London Tigers and as a sports development manager - when the opportunity arose to coach full-time.It meant leaving England to return to Lithuania, champions Ekranas appointing him assistant first-team and reserve-team coach at the end of 2010. After four years at Ekranas he was named manager of Zalgiris Vilnius, Lithuania's biggest club, where his career really took off.Dambrauskas won two league titles, three Lithuanian Cups and two Lithuanian Super Cups across three seasons - including a treble in 2016.Then came a series of moves in which Dambrauskas took charge of eight teams over nine years in seven countries. First RFS, with whom he won the Latvian Cup, and then Gorica in Croatia.A third league title came with Bulgarian side Ludogorets Razgrad, along with another Super Cup and Europa League qualification.Dambrauskas then returned to Croatia with Hajduk Split, a time which he described as "absolutely amazing" as the club won the Croatian Cup - their first trophy for 10 years.Next up was a spell in Greece with OFI Crete, then Omonia in Cyprus - who qualified for the Conference League - and Diosgyori in Hungary.Finally, in the summer of 2025, he arrived at Sabah, the 10th club of his career. Dambrauskas completed the league and cup double in his first season, as the club won the title for the first time. It took his trophy tally to 13 across five countries.Next stop, the Champions League.Dambrauskas had to navigate four knockout ties to get Sabah to the Champions League, and they are the only club to make it all the way through from the first qualifying round.Welsh club TNS, Finland's KuPS, Danish side Aarhus and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were all knocked out. The final qualifying game was as dramatic as Dambrauskas' own story.Sabah were going out, then a goal by Tellur Mutallimov in the fourth minute of stoppage time sent the tie into extra time. They went on to win 5-2 on the night and 6-4 on aggregate."To go to the Champions League is something beyond imagination," Dambrauskas said. "We have never qualified for the Conference League, we have never qualified for the Europa League. We have never passed more than two rounds in a row in one competition, and now suddenly we are here."Sabah are based in the town of Masazir - 30 miles north of the Azerbaijan capital Baku - with a population of just 19,000.Known as the Owls, Sabah were only formed in 2017 and on Tuesday will celebrate their ninth birthday.Like many small clubs, their Bank Respublika Arena home, with a capacity of less than 9,000, does not meet Uefa regulations. Instead, the club are expected to play their matches at the Olympic Stadium in Baku.Sabah will host Borussia Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli, and face a trip to Villarreal - as well as the visits to England."It can be a very hard draw, and it can be a Sabah draw," said Dambrauskas, clearly excited by the prospect."You dream for this, to play in this competition, to play against those teams. "So now is the time to show that you can handle it, to find a way to compete and we will try to do this. "We have a good team, we have an ambitious team, we have hungry players who are really keen to show themselves."Sabah president Magsud Adigozalov last week was full of praise for Dambrauskas' impact. "His influence goes beyond tactics," Adigozalov told Report. "He has instilled a mindset and winning mentality in the team. "Even in the most difficult moments, the team never abandons its game or fighting spirit, which is the result of the coach's work."Twenty years ago, Dambrauskas looked out over the pitch at Old Trafford during one of his job interviews, dreaming that one day he would stand in one of the dugouts.Now his coaching career will return to where it started."I lived in England when the battle between Manchester United and Arsenal was the biggest rivalry. Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger," Dambrauskas said. "Now I'm going to come back as a coach in the Champions League and hear that anthem. It's really amazing."

schema.headline: Manchester United v Sabah: Meet Azerbaijani club's coach Valdas Dambrauskas

title: Tanzanian President Samia's husband dies in hospital
description: The husband of Tanzania's President Samia Suluhu Hassan, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, has died while receiving treatment at a hospital in Zanzibar.Vice-presid
body: The husband of Tanzania's President Samia Suluhu Hassan, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, has died while receiving treatment at a hospital in Zanzibar.Vice-president Deogratius Ndejembi - who made the official announcement of Ameir's death - said he had been suffering from a heart condition.He was buried at his family's residence in Kizimkazi, a village on the country's semi-autonomous island of Zanzibar, on Monday evening.Ameir was an agricultural academic who largely kept a low public profile. He became Tanzania's first First Gentleman after President Samia took office in 2021.In his announcement, Ndejembi said Ameir died at 08:00 local time (06:00 GMT) on Monday at the Emilio Mzena Memorial Hospital.The vice-president led tributes as he conveyed his condolences to Samia, as well as Ameir's family and friends.Kenyan President William Ruto said he received the news of his passing with "deep sorrow"."President Samia has lost a lifelong companion, her children a beloved father, and Tanzania a distinguished son," he wrote on social media.Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema also shared his condolences, saying that they "stand side by side" with the first family, and all of Tanzania during "this difficult time".Similarly, Burundi's President Évariste Ndayishimiye paid his respects and prayed for Samia and her family to have "comfort and strength in this difficult moment"."May he [God] grant eternal rest to the soul of Hafidh Ameir Hassan," he added.The First Gentleman rarely appeared in public alongside the president. He was only occasionally seen with her at official events.He married Samia in 1978, before she entered national politics. The couple had four children - three sons and a daughter - together.Their daughter, Wanu Hafidh Ameir, is also a politician who currently serves in Zanzibar's House of Representatives in the National Assembly.

schema.headline: Tanzanian President Samia's husband dies in hospital

title: Burundians rush to leave Kenya ahead of crackdown on unregistered traders
description: Hundreds of Burundians in Kenya are scrambling to process travel documents to leave the country ahead of the crackdown on unlicensed small businesses
body: Hundreds of Burundians in Kenya are scrambling to process travel documents to leave the country ahead of the crackdown on unlicensed small businesses run by migrants.Kenyan President William Ruto set Monday as the deadline for foreigners operating small-scale businesses to cease work, after the trade ministry said some exploited visa rules to work without the required permits.Long queues were seen outside Burundi's embassy in the capital Nairobi after it said it would offer free emergency travel documents to citizens who want to go back home. Others are racing to buy bus tickets.Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of migrants from across East Africa seeking work and business opportunities.Kenya's trade ministry said there had been "deliberate misuse of visa applications by some visitors", who arrived as investors or tourists but got involved in business activities that breached their declared status.According to the United Nations refugee agency, there are around 16,000 Burundian refugees and asylum seekers in Kenya. It is unclear how many are involved in small-scale trading or how many would be affected by the crackdown.Burundians have been seen carrying all their belongings - from suitcases to mattresses - as they try to leave ahead of the crackdown, but some of them said they could not afford the cost of travel and urged the Kenyan government to extend the deadline.Ruto's directive follows a similar crackdown in Tanzania last year and rising anti‑migrant sentiment in South Africa.Burundi's Foreign Affairs Minister Edouard Bizimana said in a post on X that "Kenyans in Burundi were living peacefully but if the hate speech against Burundi continues things will certainty change"."Kenya government is responsible for the lives of Burundians living in Kenya," he added.His comments came after Ruto last week said that while Kenya remained open to foreign investment, it could not be "that a person comes from China or elsewhere to be a hawker or open a small shop".He argued that investors should create jobs and expand production rather than compete with Kenyans in small businesses.Ruto's comments sparked mixed reactions, with some critics describing them as a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia. Government officials deny the allegation.Some foreign nationals say they fear for their safety, while police have warned Kenyans against targeting them.Bizimana's post followed an urgent meeting he held with representatives of the East African Community (EAC), an eight-member bloc which promotes economic integration in the region.  Both Kenya and Burundi are part of the group. Kenyan representatives attended the meeting called by Bizimana in Burundi. Bizimana said he had asked the Kenyan ambassador to convey to his government Burundi's concerns and to ensure that no Burundian was subjected to abuse.On Sunday, a top official in Kenya's foreign affairs ministry said foreigners, with the required documentation, including "work permits and licences", could continue their activities."Burundian nationals and all East Africans - and Africans for that matter - are free to live in Kenya as long as they conduct their businesses or work according to the requirements of our laws, Permanent Secretary Korir Sing'oei said.The government's clarification, however, did little to ease concerns among some foreign traders.Alexis Ntinanirwa, the head of the Association of Burundians living in Kenya, told the BBC Great Lakes service that he was unhappy with Ruto's decision, but was urging Burundians to remain patient.He warned that the issue could have wider regional consequences because Kenyans are also involved in small-scale businesses in other East African countries."This issue is not only going to cause problems for Burundians working in Kenya, but it is also going to cause problems in the region because there are also Kenyans doing these small jobs in our countries in Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda."Ntinanirwa advised Burundians involved in hawking and other small businesses to avoid confrontation with police.Additional reporting by Akisa Wandera and Prime Ndikumagenge

schema.headline: Burundians rush to leave Kenya ahead of crackdown on unregistered traders

title: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterGrindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterGrindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal information - including their HIV status - with third parties.The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app was sued in the High Court in 2024 over claims it misused people's personal information.The class action suit was later served in the US, with the law firm leading the case saying it had signed up more than 11,000 claimants.According to a US regulatory filing, Grindr will make two £13m payments to settle the claims. The firm said the settlement includes no admission of liability.Grindr stressed the claims relate to "historical data practices" before 2020 when it was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun.The filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, external by Grindr said a settlement had been reached on 2 September."While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said in its filing.The firm has agreed to pay £13m to the counterparties by 31 December and a further £13m by 31 March 2027.'Significant distress'The claims brought more than two years ago by law firm Austen Hayes alleged Grindr had shared sensitive data with third parties for commercial purposes, breaching UK privacy laws.It said this included information about the ethnicity and sexual orientation of its users.People on Grindr have the option to share their HIV status along with when they were last tested - a move it says aims to reduce stigma, facilitate conversations and help users make informed health choices.Chaya Hanoomanjee, the lawyer who led the claim, said in April 2024 claimants had "experienced significant distress" over their sensitive and private information being shared without their consent.She said the company "owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Grindr became a publicly-listed company in 2022, two years after it was taken over by new ownersTwo data analytics services, Apptimize and Localytics, were identified as third parties with access to the sensitive data.The claim said a potentially unlimited number of third parties used it to customise advertisements to Grindr's users.It followed revelations in 2018 that Grindr had been sharing personal data, including the HIV status of its users, with the two data analytics providers.Grindr defended the practice at the time as in line with industry standards – but it said it then stopped sharing HIV data with those companies.It was fined £5.5m by Norway's data protection watchdog and, later in 2022, reprimanded by the UK Information Commissioner's Office for its data practices.The company said in its filing on Friday that since 2020, it had "overhauled" its privacy practices to help meet the "unique needs of its community"."Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control, and responsible data practices," it said.

schema.headline: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status

title: NTA: India's high-stakes exam system faces a crisis of trust
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Millions of students appear for tests conducted by India's National Testing Agency every year ByNikita YadavB
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Millions of students appear for tests conducted by India's National Testing Agency every year ByNikita YadavBBC News, DelhiIn 2017, India introduced the National Testing Agency (NTA) to conduct fair, transparent and standardised examinations. Set up under the federal education ministry, it was meant to make exams more efficient, consistent and trustworthy, after years of paper leaks, administrative errors and cheating allegations.Over the next few years, the agency took charge of some of India's largest and most competitive tests, including medical and engineering entrance examinations, university admissions and eligibility tests for teaching and research.But eight years later, the organisation created to restore trust in India's exams is facing a crisis of confidence of its own.In June, more than two million students had to retake a crucial medical entrance examination after the paper was leaked. The fallout triggered weeks of youth-led protests which eventually led to the resignation of the federal education minister.In response, the government appointed a high-level task force led by tech tycoon Nandan Nilekani to recommend reforms and restore confidence in the examination system.For many Indians, however, the announcement prompted a sense of déjà vu.A similar panel was established in 2024 after irregularities in another medical entrance examination sparked widespread unrest. That committee proposed more than 100 reforms, a little over half of which, external have reportedly been fully implemented.The cycle has repeated: an exam goes wrong, students protest, a committee is appointed and reforms are proposed - only for another crisis to expose the same weaknesses.Experts the BBC spoke to say the problems go beyond paper leaks - from NTA's accountability and capacity to exam centralisation, design and whether India's high-stakes testing system needs a rethink.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than two million students appeared for the NEET-UG retest BJ Rao, who was part of the 2024 panel and is now head of SGT University near Delhi, says India should move more decisively towards computer-based examinations to minimise the chances of paper leaks, increase efficiency and reduce human involvement wherever possible."Digital connectivity has vastly improved across the country, what we need to do is put in resources and focus on upgrading infrastructure and move to computer-based exams," he told the BBC."We currently have ad hoc centres for conducting exams. We need to replace them with standardised state-controlled online centres."But technology alone will not solve the problem, he says. Rao points to the NTA's reliance on contract staff: just 24 of its 221 employees are permanent, with many from bureaucratic backgrounds, according to the government."When you have a large portion of people who work on a temporary basis then there is no sense of belonging, and that has an impact on the functions as well. You need people who are well-versed in academia and experienced in conducting such assessments to ensure better management and oversight," he explains. Some experts argue that repeated crises have exposed flaws not only in how exams are conducted, but also in how they are designed.Keshav Aggarwal, an educationist and president of Educators Federation, says the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate) or NEET-UG - whose paper leak triggered this year's protests - could be restructured along the lines of the country's engineering entrance examination, which is computer-based and conducted in two stages.Rather than relying on a single high-stakes test day, the exams could be held across multiple sessions with different sets of questions, he says. "Different stages and days with varying sets of questions" would reduce the risks associated with any one examination and make the system more resilient to disruptions, Aggarwal explains.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, The NEET-UG paper leak triggered massive protests in India Experts also question whether an annual exam can work when millions compete for limited university places.India needs a system where students can take important entrance exams more than once a year, as is common in some western countries, said Yamini Aiyar, senior visiting fellow at Brown University."This would give students another chance if an exam is cancelled or they do not perform well, reducing the risk of losing an entire year," she says.For millions of Indian students, the risk is real. Many spend years preparing and tens of thousands of rupees on private tuition. A leaked, cancelled or delayed exam can suddenly upend months or years of preparation.Pari, 17, experienced that uncertainty first-hand. After taking NEET this year, she had to retake it after the original exam was cancelled following a paper leak."It was very frustrating. All our preparation had gone to waste, and we had to start all over again," she said.The experience left her angry at repeated exam failures."The government can form as many panels as it likes. We need a system strong enough to prevent paper leaks from happening again."Mansi Bansal, 23, has a similar story. She spent months preparing for UGC-NET, a qualification for entry-level college teaching jobs.The exam was cancelled after a 2024 paper leak and again this year after the NTA cited errors in three subjects.Bansal took the affected commerce paper and will retest on 9 September."I put my life on hold all these months, stopping going to the gym, hanging out with friends or even attending family gatherings," she said. "I had planned my entire year but now it has all gone into uncertainty. Can the government promise a leak won't happen again?"Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, Student activists and opposition parties have been demanding to scrap the NTA Such experiences have fuelled calls from student activists and opposition politicians to scrap the NTA altogether.Educationists argue that scrapping the agency would not solve the underlying problem.The NTA needs deep structural reform to address recurring failures, but abolishing it is not the answer, said M Jagadesh Kumar, former chairman of India's universities regulator."A single national testing body offers common security standards, technology, candidate services and result procedures. Creating many new agencies could duplicate costs and produce uneven safeguards," he told PTI news agency.Rao agrees."It is not a case of all bad news. The body has conducted several exams successfully, where we did not hear of any leaks," he said.What is needed, he argues, is a statutory institution staffed by specialists with the academic, technical and operational expertise to run a secure examination system.Yet for some experts, the debate ultimately goes beyond the NTA itself.Aiyar says the bigger issue is not just stopping the next paper leak, but whether a highly centralised testing system can cope with the intense competition for limited educational opportunities.The NTA may be able to make exams more secure, she says. "But it cannot, at least on its own, change a system in which millions of students compete for a limited number of seats and a single exam can shape their future."Some experts say reform must go beyond the NTA itself: India needs an exam system less reliant on one-off, high-stakes tests, gives students multiple chances and can better withstand disruptions.Rao remains optimistic that the task force led by Nilekani will help plug gaps in the existing system.But for many students, another committee offers little reassurance unless it produces changes they can actually see."I am studying for my university entrance examination next year," said a 16-year-old Grade 12 student. "In my head I am prepared that there might be a leak. But what can we do about it? I will prepare and hope for the best."

schema.headline: NTA: India's high-stakes exam system faces a crisis of trust

title: Satya Niketan: Rescuers dig through debris as seven dead in building collapse in Delhi
description: Rescuers are digging through the rubble a day after a residential building collapsed in the Indian capital, Delhi, killing at least seven people.It's
body: Rescuers are digging through the rubble a day after a residential building collapsed in the Indian capital, Delhi, killing at least seven people.It's not clear how many people were inside the five-storey building in south-west Delhi - or if there are still people under the debris.Eyewitnesses told local media on Sunday that two-to-four dozen people were inside, but no official numbers have been shared. Authorities have confirmed 12 people were taken to hospital and that seven died while others are receiving treatment.Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said "accumulation of water, combined with ongoing repair work in the basement" of the building, Hostel Daze, caused the collapse. The building owner has been arrested and five senior civic officials of Delhi Municipal Corporation (MCD) have been suspended following the tragedy, Gupta added.The building in the Satya Niketan neighbourhood of south-west Delhi, which sits a short distance from Delhi University's south campus which has five colleges, came down around 13:30 local time (08:00 GMT) on Sunday. A majority of the residents were students and many were thought to be in their rooms at the time of the collapse as there were no lessons on Sunday.On Monday morning, Gupta said "approximately 80% of the debris had been cleared" from the building, and "only the rubble from the basement remains". The BBC found the area around the site of the collapse cordoned off and teeming with rescue workers in bright orange uniforms. An excavator dug through the rubble in the hope of finding survivors amidst a pile of bricks. In another corner, a few mattresses half covered in debris were lying in a pile.The smell of burning metal was overpowering as teams of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) could be seen using electric saws to cut through iron grills, penetrating layers and layers of steel and concrete. There is no confirmation if there are still people under the debris or if there are more survivors. Hospital officials are not saying whether the casualties include students, local residents or labourers who were working in the basement.On Sunday, a local legislative assembly member at the scene said that some of the trapped students had been making calls from under the rubble.An eyewitness who was at his shop nearby when the tragedy struck told news agency ANI that the building collapse sounded "like the rumble of an earthquake". "We rushed out immediately; there was a lot of smoke and dust here. The entire building had collapsed. Some bodies were recovered, and they also rescued four students who were still breathing." He said he could hear students crying out from under the rubble saying "save us, save us!"Gupta said an adjacent building had been evacuated "as a precautionary measure" - and local media reports say it would be demolished on Monday."Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped," she added.Delhi Police said the building had only been 40 or 50 years old.The owner of a nearby shop told ANI that it had been under a 100-year lease and that the leaseholder had undertaken excavation work in the basement to expand the hostel and increase their income.A civic official said they were trying to ascertain whether any digging or structural work was carried out in the building recently, Times of India reported., external"Given the incessant rain, we are examining the possibility of seepage weakening the structure. Repair or other work could also have contributed to the collapse. At this stage, however, it is difficult to establish the exact cause," he said.Police have registered a case against the owner of the building and are searching for him.The National Students' Union of India called on the government to investigate the cause of the collapse and hold anyone found responsible to account."Negligence with the safety of students and common people will not be tolerated at any cost," it said.Satya Niketan is a densely populated area which houses a large student population, with a number of hostels in the neighbourhood.Many students who come from outside Delhi to attend South Campus colleges are forced to live in cheap private hostels and paying-guest (PG) accommodations due to a lack of hostel facilities on campus."There are 75 students in Sociology Honours class, but only two get a seat in the college hostel. All other students have to live here," Sawai Sharma, a student of Venkateswara College, told BBC News Hindi. Sharma, who often visited a friend who lived in the building and narrowly escaped the accident, said a bed in the building cost 18,000 rupees ($190; £140) a month, making it affordable for students.Another student, Shivam Yadav, said a friend of his lived in the building and was in his room at the time of the accident. "He was on the third floor at the time of the accident. He has been rescued and sent to hospital."Yadav said that most of the buildings in Satya Niketan are "overloaded". "The buildings are in a dilapidated condition. No inspections are conducted. There are no rules or guidelines here."College student Ankit Tiwari said conditions at these hostels and PGs "are appalling". "Students are paying a lot for a very small space which they share with others. There is no proper water or sewage facility here." Tiwari, who lives nearby, reached the site about half an hour after the collapse. "Students were helping each other as we came first, before the rescue teams arrived. What we saw was tragic. We have been finding books, mangled desks and study notes," he said.Building collapses are relatively common in Delhi, with more than a thousand recorded in the past three years causing dozens of deaths, according to fire department figures. Poor foundations, inadequate materials and unqualified construction workers were among the common reasons for collapses.Eleven people, including three children, were reportedly killed last April when a residential building collapsed in north-eastern Delhi.In 2024, three students drowned after getting trapped in the flooded basement of an exam coaching centre in capital Delhi, sparking anger and protests.Additional reporting from Aleks Phillips

schema.headline: Satya Niketan: Rescuers dig through debris as seven dead in building collapse in Delhi
